history.heading: Settlement and colonisation
paragraphs: The Solomon Islands, a chain of nearly 1,000 islands in the southwestern Pacific, have been inhabited for at least 30,000 years. Austronesian peoples arrived later. Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña arrived in 1568 and named the islands after King Solomon, hoping they held gold.
In the 19th century many islanders were recruited or kidnapped ("blackbirding") to work on plantations in Australia and Fiji. Britain declared a protectorate in 1893.

history.heading: War and independence
paragraphs: The Battle of Guadalcanal (1942–43) was a turning point in the Pacific War. The Solomon Islands became independent on 7 July 1978. Ethnic conflict between groups from Guadalcanal and Malaita ("the Tensions", 1998–2003) led to an Australian-led regional intervention (RAMSI) from 2003 to 2017. Riots in Honiara in 2021 were linked to tensions over the government's switch of diplomatic recognition to China.

culture.heading: Melanesian culture
paragraphs: English is official, but Solomon Islands Pidgin is the common language among over 70 local languages. Most people are Christian. Shell money, carving and panpipe music are traditions. Custom (kastom) and kinship (wantok) are central to society.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: The Solomon Islands is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Governments are often unstable coalitions. In 2019 it switched recognition from Taiwan to China and in 2022 signed a security agreement with China, raising concerns in Australia and the United States.

economy.heading: Logging and fishing
paragraphs: Most people depend on subsistence farming and fishing. Timber from logging, often unsustainable, has been the main export, along with fish, palm oil and copra. Gold mining has resumed. The country is one of the poorest in the Pacific. The currency is the Solomon Islands dollar.
